# Alpha

> [!tldr] In 3 lines
> Alpha is the base idea of this course.
> It is the thing the next concept builds on.
> Every exercise in the course starts from it.

## Study explanation

Alpha is the first idea of the course. It is simple on purpose: everything later rests on it, so
a mistake here shows up everywhere else. The course introduces it with a worked example and then
asks for it without notes, which is the pattern the whole course follows.

The most common mistake is to treat Alpha as a definition to memorize instead of an idea to use.
If you can say why it matters in the next lesson but cannot use it in a new problem, the idea is
not there yet.

## Key takeaways

- **Remember:** Alpha is the base idea, and the next concept needs it.
- **Common confusion:** Alpha is not the name of a fact to recite, it is the thing you apply.
- **Exercise:** write, without notes, one problem that uses Alpha, and say which step of it needed the idea.

# Beta

> [!tldr] In 3 lines
> Beta is the second idea of the course.
> It needs Alpha, so Alpha comes first.
> The course shows it in a problem you have not seen.

## Study explanation

Beta is the second idea of the course, and it cannot be understood without Alpha: every problem
that uses Beta starts from the step Alpha teaches. That is why the course orders the concepts by
necessity and not by chapter, and why the concept map marks Alpha as the prerequisite of Beta.

The most common mistake is to meet Beta with a definition and no base. The learner sees the
words, repeats them, and then fails on the first problem that asks for a decision.

## Key takeaways

- **Remember:** Beta needs Alpha, and the problems are where Beta shows up.
- **Common confusion:** reading Beta twice is not knowing Alpha.
- **Exercise:** solve one Beta problem and name the step that used Alpha.
